what_it_does: Modern chips are increasingly built by bonding multiple smaller dies (chiplets) face-to-face using copper-to-copper (Cu-Cu) hybrid bonding, a packaging technique that connects chips with microscopic copper pads instead of solder bumps, enabling much denser interconnects. This bonding process is sensitive to several real-world imperfections: tiny misalignments between the two dies (overlay errors), stray particles on the surface, slight recesses in the copper pads, surface roughness at the nanoscale, and uneven copper density across the die. Any of these can cause a bond to fail, reducing the fraction of chips that work (yield). Simulating all these defects together using the standard Monte Carlo method (running thousands of random trials) is accurate but extremely slow. YAP replaces that simulation with a fast analytical model — a set of equations that directly compute yield from the defect parameters — achieving results that match Monte Carlo simulation while running roughly 10,000 times faster, making it practical to sweep many design choices during early-stage chip packaging design.
